headline: The West Cut Is Loading Bunker and Blues Are Cashing In
subhead: Moriches Inlet's main channel is running deeper and tighter to the west jetty than it was in June — and the bait knows it.
body_markdown:
I walked the west jetty at Cupsogue on the last of the outgoing Tuesday morning and the current line told me everything I needed to know. The main scour channel has tightened up against the rocks — I'd guess it's pushed another ten, fifteen yards west since the spring blow reshaped things back in April. That's not unusual for this inlet. Moriches doesn't sit still. Every big northeast blow moves sand around inside that throat, and this year the deeper water is hugging the jetty tighter than it has in a couple seasons. What that means practically: the current is running harder and faster through a narrower slot, and anything moving bait through that cut is getting squeezed into a smaller, more concentrated lane. Bass, blues, whatever's out there — they don't have to work as hard to find the conveyor belt. They just sit on the edge of it.

And there's plenty riding that conveyor belt right now. We flagged this last week — said the bluefish blitz was coming as bunker pushed along the south shore beaches — and it's here. Cupsogue and the ocean beach stretch east toward Pikes Beach have had bunker schools pinned tight to the bar most mornings, and the blues have been working them hard enough to see it from the dune line. Birds diving, bunker getting nervous and bunching, then that telltale slick of oil and scale on the surface. If you're fishing the beach, get there at first light before the wind builds — poppers and metal, Ava 27s and 40s in bare or teaser-dressed, cast into the edge of the bait ball, not the middle of it. Blues in the 4 to 8 pound class, some bigger mixed in, and they're not fussy right now. The bite's been reliable enough that I'd call it the most dependable action in the zone this week, but it's also short-lived most mornings — an hour, hour and a half before the sun gets up and the bunker scatter into deeper water.

Striped bass is a different story, and it's the same story we're seeing up and down the coast this time of year. Surface water in the bay and along the beach has settled into that mid-70s range that pushes stripers off the daytime program entirely. I fished the inlet on an evening high this week and didn't touch a bass until the light was mostly gone — then had three fish in about forty minutes, all in that 26 to 30 inch window, working bucktails tipped with white Gulp along the deeper edge of that west channel scour, right where the current drops off into 12, 14 feet. That's the pattern to lean on right now: dusk into full dark, working the deeper cuts inside the inlet or the channel edges off Tuthill Point on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, when bait gets flushed out of the bay and funnels through that narrower western slot. Don't waste daylight hours on bass here unless you're fishing deep bay structure — the flats are too warm, fish have pulled off them.

Fluke are around but it's a grind, not a program. The bay-side humps off Smith Point and the deeper holes inside the inlet proper are holding fish, but you're sorting through a lot of shorts to find keepers. I had a decent day drifting the channel edge near the Coast Guard station with 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, and the better fish — one going close to 5 pounds — came off the deeper side of the drift where the bottom drops from 8 feet to about 14 on the edge of the old scour hole. That deeper, cooler water is where the quality fish are sitting this time of year, same pattern you're seeing everywhere from here to the Great South Bay. Weakfish have been scarce for me this week — a few reports of fish coming out of the deeper bay channels near Pattersquash, but nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet.

Porgies are steady if unspectacular around the bridge structure and the bay side of the inlet rocks — bloodworms and squid strips on a hi-lo rig will keep you busy on the bottom stages of the tide, decent eating-size fish mixed with the usual shorts.

Looking ahead: as long as this bait stays pinned to the beach and the weather holds stable, I expect the bluefish blitz to keep running the ocean side through the week — that's the surest bet going right now. If we get a wind shift out of the southwest that pushes hard for a couple days, watch for that bunker to scatter and push into the bay itself, which could actually improve things for bass and weakfish on the inside if the bait relocates rather than disperses entirely. For bass, I'd keep working the dusk-to-dark window at the inlet's deeper cuts — that's where the fish are stacking with the water this warm, and until we get a real cooldown or a stretch of onshore wind that mixes the water column, that nighttime program is going to be the reliable one. Cupsogue at first light for blues, the inlet after dark for bass — that's my week, and it's a decent split if you've got the stamina for both ends of the day.
